newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus election chief says referendum invalid.
newsitem.headline: Belarus election chief says referendum invalid.

text.p: Belarus's top electoral official on Monday described a referendum in which President Alexander Lukashenko is seeking to broaden his powers as a "national disgrace" and said he would not validate the results.

Viktor Gonchar, responsible for monitoring and organising voting in the former Soviet republic, was elected to his post by parliament which, like the constitutional court and his Central Commission on Elections and Referendums, opposes Lukashenko.

"While I am in this post, the law in this state will be obeyed. I can state today that I will not sign a final protocol on the referendum," he told deputies and regional leaders meeting in parliament as "early" voting entered its third day.
"If anyone thinks they can carry out a referendum by their own rules, by decrees which contradict constitutional court rulings, they are quite wrong," he added.
Lukashenko, 42, who has muzzled the press and regularly ignores rulings by other branches of power, has attracted criticism from the West for his increasingly authoritarian rule.
A former state farm chief, he enjoys broad support in rural areas for his anti-corruption, pro-Moscow stance which won him a landslide victory in July 1994.
By law, Gonchar would have to approve the results of the referendum as fair and free for them to be put into effect, but Lukashenko regularly ignores rulings by the country's rival branches of power.
The president has incurred the wrath of a majority of parliamentarians, the court and electoral authorities for decreeing the results of the vote will be legally binding.
Parliament, backed by the constitutional court, had decided the results of the referendum should only be advisory and have no legal force, in line with the constitution.

Lukashenko is seeking approval for a new constitution under which he would extend his term by more than two years, create an upper chamber of parliament partly appointed by him, and name half the constitutional court and electoral commission.
Deputies are proposing their own draft constitution which would abolish the presidency in its present form and strengthen parliament's authority.
Each side in the row, compared by some analysts to a legal stalemate in Russia in 1993 which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament, accuses the other of breaking the law.
Gonchar said none of the votes cast would be counted until copies of the draft constitutions had been delivered to polling stations. "What is happening is a national disgrace," he said.
He described the staff of state-controlled Belarussian television, which has been broadcasting appeals to the nation to vote any day up to and including November 24, as "crazy people".
Advance voting, which began on Saturday, is intended only for those who cannot make it on the official day.
The electorate of 7.6 million of a population of about 10 million is to answer a confusing seven questions at the poll.
Four were proposed by Lukashenko -- his draft constitution, on banning the death penalty, on land reform and on changing the date of the national holiday.

Deputies' questions, apart from their draft constitution, seek approval for direct elections of local leaders rather than having them appointed by the president and for funding of public bodies from the state budget.
One deputy, Viktor Khomich, showed journalists a sample voting paper he said he had found at a polling station.
In it, the answers were already filled out in Lukashenko's favour -- for his draft, for continued use of the death penalty and against all three questions proposed by parliament.
